# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Respondents → the public account each story is based on

- Dwayne Hollis → [LYC] the group is "superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.)": an assistant super writes the log (the Current-solution escape). Author's invention beyond that.

Contractor operations leads (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

screens.instead: Which step do you believe slows the purchase most? A trial on one live job / A check that it works with Procore / A security review / A budget approval

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step I'd want, it makes sense for Keel to show me the belief it will test about that step, as the last of the commercial checks.
screens.why2: "Paid pilot on one site" is how I sell and talk, and the bar of no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no reads clearly the first time.
screens.why3: A superintendent can't start a paid pilot, because we charge the general contractor per site and I told Keel the contractor's operations lead decides, so this tests a commitment the supers have no power to make.
screens.why4: The screen is a drafted belief and a bar to read, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: I gave this step for the buyer, but Keel changed the subject to "most construction superintendents", which contradicts my who-decides answer even though "paid pilot on one site" is kept.
screens.instead: Belief to test: Most contractor operations leads would start a paid pilot on one site now. Bar: holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.

screens.why1: I have just set my first real step of a paid pilot on one site, so being asked whether to offer a pilot before the study goes out follows naturally.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" and the hint are plain words, but it does not say what the pilot is or who would be asked, so I need a second read to see whether this is my paid one-site pilot, and whether the supers or the contractor's ops lead can ask to join.
screens.why3: Whether I want to offer a pilot is my own call as founder, and I am already chasing commercial GCs for pilots.
screens.why4: The only choice I can see is "Continue", so offering versus skipping is not laid out as a clear choice and I cannot tell which one Continue records, though skipping an optional step is covered.
screens.why5: It keeps the word pilot and says nothing changes people's answers, but it does not tie back to "start a paid pilot on one site", so it drifts from my step into a generic pilot and I cannot tell if the paid part or the per-site term carries through.
screens.instead: Offer your paid pilot on one site to the people who finish this study? They can ask to join after they have answered, and nothing here changes their answers. [Yes, offer it] [No, not on this study]

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, it makes obvious sense to settle who will put the questions to my superintendents.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but 'runs on its own AI', 'Keel's credits' and the picked 'face' are product terms a construction-software founder needs a second read to connect, and the hint does not say what I am actually choosing between.
screens.why3: I know my superintendents and can judge whether they would tap through questions in the trailer or talk to an AI interviewer, so this is my call to make.
screens.why4: As recorded, the choice is to lock a preselected face, which leaves the read-and-tap route described in the hint unclear as an option and does not show what happens without credits.
screens.why5: It keeps my segment, superintendents at US general contractors, exactly as I typed it, and changes nothing about my idea.
screens.instead: Who should ask superintendents at US general contractors your questions? Options: 'They read the questions and tap their answers (free)' / 'An AI interviewer asks them out loud, using this face (uses Keel credits)'.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it makes obvious sense to settle how my superintendents will answer.
screens.why2: The choices are clear, but the AI option's accuracy line is packed and clipped, and "needs Keel's credits" and the stray "Hear it" take a second read.
screens.why3: I know supers work from phones in loud trailers and on noisy sites, so I can judge which format would suit them.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct, but the AI option's accuracy claim is worded oddly, with "Every answer in a quiet room" reading like a fragment.
screens.why5: My "Text only" choice is shown as typed and nothing about Fresco or my roles is changed.
screens.instead: How should they answer? AI interviewer: a face on video asks each question aloud and they talk, type or tap (we catch every answer in a quiet room, more than 9 in 10 on a loud site; uses Keel credits). Text only: they read each question and tap or type. Let them choose: they pick when they open the link (uses Keel credits).

screens.why1: After choosing how they answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who gets the link.
screens.why2: The question and the choices between named people, a Keel search and one open link read plainly to me on first pass, and the 'Contacts page' is clear enough as a part of the tool.
screens.why3: I know which supers I can reach, whether by name through the general contractors we ask for introductions to or through a group where they already gather.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people, but the screen doesn't say how my two kinds of people, the superintendents and the contractor operations leads, are handled when each needs a separate link.
screens.why5: Nothing here alters what I typed, and 'People I know by name' keeps my answer of sending to each person by name.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? Keep the three options, and add under them: 'You'll do this once for the superintendents and once for the contractor operations leads.'

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check straight away whether our jobs run on these platforms, since that decides whether the study applies to me.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are everyday words in my trade, but "the superintendents you decide for" is not how I'd say it, and I had to read it twice to see it meant the supers whose software I pick and pay for.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our job-site software, so I know exactly which platforms our supers' jobs run on.
screens.why4: Yes and No are clear and a gate has no escape by rule, but a contractor with some jobs on Procore or ACC and some on something else has no clean answer beyond a generous Yes.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of superintendents on Procore or ACC, and no product or plan reaches me, though "you decide for" is slightly survey-speak rather than a leak.
screens.why6: It is short and one question and says well, but "the construction superintendents you decide for" is a slight mouthful on one hearing and ACC only works if I already know it, which I do.
screens.instead: Do any of your company's jobs run on Procore or ACC? Yes; No

screens.why1: After confirming my supers' jobs run on Procore or ACC, showing me the idea before asking whether I'd buy it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, assignees, due dates, action items, Procore and ACC are all everyday words in my job, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know how my supers walk sites, log the day and chase the crew on action items, so I can picture this on my own jobs.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks where it should not, but the closing belief line only repeats the card, and its 'a record sent to Procore or ACC' doesn't quite say whether this fills the daily log, which is what I'd need to know.
screens.why6: It says fine in short sentences and 'ACC' is a name I say anyway, but the last sentence re-lists what I just heard and 'notes with photos, assignees and due dates' is a lot to hold at once.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco. During the site walk, your superintendents take short videos and talk over them. Fresco turns them into notes with photos, assignees and due dates, and texts the crew their action items. Your superintendents then send the notes to Procore or ACC in one click. The people building it believe it would save superintendents the evening write-up.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, what the daily log costs us now is an obvious thing to ask someone who pays for the tools, though it does not name which sites or say it means the time spent on the log itself.
screens.why2: "Daily log" and "per site" are my everyday words, but "lose to" leaves me a second read on whether it means all the time spent on the log or only the wasted part.
screens.why3: As ops lead I know how many sites we run and what the supers do, but I don't track log hours per site, so my number would be an estimate built from what supers tell me.
screens.why4: The number box and the two chips cover the true answers, but "Nothing" is odd next to a typed 0 and the screen shows two escapes where the rule allows one, "I can't recall" being the set wording for this question type.
screens.why5: It stays on the founder's daily log and superintendent's site work, and nothing of the product or the founder's terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It says well as one short question, but "how many hours per site" over a month is a sum to work out on hearing, and the spoken escape "I don't know" differs from the set "I can't recall" and drops the "Nothing" chip on screen.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many hours did one superintendent spend on the daily log at a typical site? Type a number, or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the hours lost to the daily log, it makes sense to ask what this is worth to me, since I'm the one who pays.
screens.why2: "Worth to you a month, per site" is how I already budget job-site software, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for these tools by the site, so I can answer from what we pay now and what those hours cost us.
screens.why4: The bands share their edges at $800 and $2,500, and "Under $500" is the only band for anything cheaper, so a $100 answer and a $450 answer look the same, though the "I wouldn't pay" and "I can't say" exits both fit.
screens.why5: "Imagine Fresco" is the idea card shown on purpose, and nothing else about the founder's plan or their terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: Six dollar ranges in one breath, each repeating "per site a month", is too much to hold after one hearing, and the guidelines say to ask price's six rungs in two steps when spoken.
screens.instead: What would Fresco be worth to you per site each month: under $500; $500 to $799; $800 to $2,499; $2,500 to $5,000; over $5,000; or I wouldn't pay for this? Or say I can't say. (When spoken, first ask: under $800, $800 or more, or I wouldn't pay for this? Then read only the bands in that range.)

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, it is obvious why they would ask what would push it higher.
screens.why2: Short plain words that I can answer on first read, and Fresco is the name from the idea card I was just shown.
screens.why3: I can say what I would pay more for from what I know of running job sites, but it is a guess about a product I have only seen on a card, not something I have used.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: Fresco and the price are what I was shown and what I picked, so nothing new from the founder reaches me and the meaning holds.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but "$500 to $800 per site a month" is a mouthful of numbers to hear in one breath, though it is my own answer so I would follow it.

screens.why1: After pricing it makes sense to ask how a tool like this gets paid for, but the jump from what would make it worth more to the last tool we bought is a little abrupt.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and other spending are how I already talk about paying for software, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our job-site software, so I know where the money came from on the last tool.
screens.why4: The first three are clear and the escape fits, but 'There was no budget for it' overlaps with 'Taken from other spending', because a tool we paid for with no budget still got paid from somewhere.
screens.why5: Nothing about Fresco or the founder's terms shows up here; it is a plain question about how we paid for a past tool.
screens.why6: It is short and there are four brief options I can hold after hearing them once, though the two sentences at the start are one setup and one question, which still says fine.
screens.instead: Think of the last tool your team paid for. Where did the money come from? A budget line we already had; A new budget line someone signed off; Or taken from other spending. Or say I can't recall one.

screens.why1: I just put this at $500 to $800 per site and said where the money comes from, so asking whether I could approve the top of that range is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Sign off, per site and CFO are how I talk about spending, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our job-site software, so I know exactly what I can approve alone and when it has to go up the line.
screens.why4: The answers cover my real situations, but the CFO is also 'someone else', and 'I can't recall one' doesn't fit because this asks what I could do, not about something I'd have to remember.
screens.why5: It uses the $800 from my own answer and my own kind of approval chain, with no product name or founder's terms leaking in.
screens.why6: It's short and the four options are easy to hold, but 'Or say I can't recall one' sounds wrong after a could-you question, and the 'No, the CFO' answer has to be matched to an either-or question.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $800 per site a month yourself, or not? Yes, on my own; No, the CFO would decide; No, several people would decide; No, another person would decide; or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after who signs off on the money, it makes sense to ask what else stands between me and buying, and a Procore check is the obvious one.
screens.why2: I know what a Procore integration check is, but "a check" doesn't say whether it means IT, Procore or my team, and "went through" is a bit loose, so I'd need a second to settle on what's being asked.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our site software, so I know whether a new tool has to be proven against Procore first and roughly how long that takes.
screens.why4: The three answers are distinct and cover it, but "I can't recall" is an odd escape for a what-if about a tool I haven't bought, where the honest answer is that I can't tell yet.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, since Fresco is the name from the idea card, but the founder's jobs run on Procore or ACC and this drops ACC, leaving out anyone whose sites run on it.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short question with three short options I can hold, and the escape comes last, so I could answer straight away.
screens.instead: If you bought Fresco, would someone have to check it works with your Procore or ACC setup first? Yes, and it would take a long time; Yes, but it would be quick; No, no check needed; or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Coming right after the sign-off and Procore-check questions, it is an obvious place to ask what else would hold up the purchase.
screens.why2: It is short and plain, and I can answer it first time in the words I'd use about buying software.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our job-site tools, so I know what holds up a purchase like this: IT review, contract terms, getting the supers on board.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options or chips to judge.
screens.why5: Fresco is the name from the idea card I was already shown, so nothing new leaks and no founder's term reaches me that I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says well aloud, and I can hear it once and just answer.

screens.why1: Last question of the buying part, after price, sign-off and what would slow it down, so asking whether I'd actually start a pilot is the obvious close.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site is how I'd normally try a tool on a job, so I get it on first read with no odd words.
screens.why3: I decide on and pay for this software, so whether I'd pay to try it on one site is my call to make.
screens.why4: The set is complete and the floor of No fits with no escape needed, but it is lopsided, with a firm yes, a probably not and a no, and no 'probably yes' for someone leaning in who still has conditions.
screens.why5: Fresco is the name from the idea card I was already shown, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me here.
screens.why6: One short question with three short options that I can hold after one hearing, and the only repeat is the phrase paid pilot on one site, which still says easily.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you start a paid pilot on one site, or not? Yes, I'd start one; Probably, with conditions; Probably not; or No.
